pos: n. (proper, the country the Philistines came from)
etymology: Hebrew Kaphtor, commonly identified with Crete or the Aegean coastlands. The Authorized Version names it three times, and each names it as the origin of Israel's most persistent enemy.
biblical_def: Moses records an older displacement as he rehearses Israel's borders: “And the Avims which dwelt in Hazerim, even unto Azzah, the Caphtorims, which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their stead” (Deuteronomy 2:23). Jeremiah names the same country in his oracle against the Philistines: “for the LORD will spoil the Philistines, the remnant of the country of Caphtor” (Jeremiah 47:4). The great verse is Amos's, and it is aimed squarely at Israel's complacency: “Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the LORD. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?” (Amos 9:7). God claims to have conducted the migrations of the Philistines and the Syrians as truly as he conducted the exodus. Israel's uniqueness was never that God moved them; it was the covenant, and Amos says so to a people who had confused the two.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the country from which the Caphtorim and the Philistines came forth.
webster_full: PHILISTINE, n. One of an ancient people who occupied the sea coast of Canaan and were long the enemies of Israel.
MIGRATION, n. The act of removing from one kingdom or state to another, for the purpose of permanent residence.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; foresight; timely care.
NATION, n. A body of people inhabiting the same country, or united under the same sovereign or government.
ELECTION, n. In theology, the choice of persons to eternal life; divine choice; predetermination of God.

Amos 9:7

Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the LORD. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?
Amos 9:8
Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: God's particular love for his people is regularly turned into a claim of national superiority; Amos answers that by telling Israel God also brought the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 9:7 is one of the most bracing verses in the prophets and it cuts in two directions at once. To an Israel that treated the exodus as proof of its own worth, God says he has conducted other nations' migrations too — the Philistines from Caphtor, the Syrians from Kir — and asks whether they are not to him as the children of the Ethiopians. Election is not a compliment paid to a superior people. Deuteronomy had already said the LORD did not set his love upon them because they were more in number, for they were the fewest of all people, but because he loved them.

The verse cuts the other way as well, and the next verse proves it: Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the LORD. The covenant is real and it holds. What Amos demolishes is the inference that a people who are loved may therefore sin safely. God governs every nation's history, judges his own people first, and keeps his promise to a remnant — three things a comfortable religion would rather not hold together.

pos: n. (proper, a son of Ishmael; father of the Ituraeans)
etymology: Hebrew Yetuwr, probably an enclosure or encampment. He is one of the twelve princes of Ishmael, and his descendants are the Ituraeans whose region Luke names in dating the ministry of John the Baptist.
biblical_def: Jetur is named among the twelve sons of Ishmael in Genesis: “Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah” (Genesis 25:15), a list the Chronicler repeats: “Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael” (1 Chronicles 1:31). God had promised Abraham concerning Ishmael that he would make him a great nation and that twelve princes should he beget, and the genealogies are the record of that promise kept to a son who was not the son of the covenant. Centuries later the tribes descended from him meet Israel in war: “And they made war with the Hagarites, with Jetur, and Nephish, and Nodab” (1 Chronicles 5:19), and the account adds that the Reubenites and Gadites cried to God in the battle and he was intreated of them, because they put their trust in him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, whose descendants warred with the trans-Jordan tribes.
webster_full: ISHMAELITE, n. A descendant of Ishmael, the son of Abraham by Hagar; a dweller in the wilderness.
ITURAEA, n. A region northeast of Palestine, named in Luke 3 as part of the tetrarchy of Philip.
PRINCE, n. A sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation or state; a chief of a tribe.
PROMISE, n. In Scripture, a declaration of God which he binds himself to fulfil, and which faith lays hold of.
INTREAT, v.t. To ask earnestly; to beseech; and in the passive, to be prevailed upon by entreaty.

corruption_summary: God's promises to those outside the covenant line are overlooked, as though his faithfulness were confined to the elect people; Ishmael received a promise of twelve princes and the genealogies prove it kept.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps his word even where no covenant of grace is in view. He told Abraham concerning Ishmael, twelve princes shall he beget, and I will make him a great nation, and Genesis 25 lists the twelve by name, Jetur among them. The lists that readers hurry past are the documentary evidence that God does what he says. A God who is meticulous about a promise made to the son who was sent away is a God to be trusted about promises made to sons who are kept.

1 Chronicles 5 supplies the other half. The descendants of Jetur become enemies, and Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh go to war with them. The Chronicler is careful about why the battle went as it did: they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them, because they put their trust in him. Right relation to God is not settled by ancestry on either side. Ishmael's line received real temporal blessing and stood outside the covenant; Israel's line had the covenant and still had to trust.

pos: n. (proper, a son of Abraham by Keturah; also a Canaanite whose daughter Judah married)
etymology: Hebrew Shuwach, a pit or depression. Two men bear the name, and keeping them apart matters: one is Abraham's son by Keturah, ancestor of Bildad the Shuhite; the other is the Canaanite father-in-law of Judah.
biblical_def: The first Shuah is the last named of Keturah's six sons: “And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah” (Genesis 25:2). Abraham gave gifts to these sons and sent them eastward, away from Isaac, while Isaac received all that he had. From this line comes Bildad the Shuhite, one of Job's three friends. The second Shuah is a Canaanite, and the marriage is recorded as a step downward: “And Judah saw there a daughter of a certain Canaanite, whose name was Shuah; and he took her, and went in unto her” (Genesis 38:2). That marriage produced Er, Onan and Shelah, and Genesis 38 goes on to Tamar, the two sons who died, and the twins Pharez and Zarah. “And in process of time the daughter of Shuah Judah's wife died” (Genesis 38:12) is the verse that sets the rest of that grim chapter in motion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a son of Abraham by Keturah, and separately as a Canaanite whose daughter Judah married.
webster_full: KETURAH, n. The wife whom Abraham took after the death of Sarah, and the mother of six sons.
CONCUBINE, n. A woman who cohabits with a man without being his lawful wife; in Scripture, a secondary wife of inferior rank.
SHUHITE, n. A descendant of Shuah the son of Abraham; the designation of Bildad, one of Job's friends.
CANAANITE, n. A descendant of Canaan the son of Ham; one of the peoples whose daughters Israel was forbidden to marry.
LINEAGE, n. Race; progeny; descendants in a line from a common progenitor.

corruption_summary: Marriage is now judged almost entirely by attraction and compatibility, and Genesis 38 opens with Judah seeing a Canaanite woman and taking her — a sentence written in the same grammar the chapter goes on to indict.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 38:2 is written to be noticed: And Judah saw there a daughter of a certain Canaanite... and he took her. Saw, took — the grammar of Eve at the tree and of David on the roof. The chapter that follows is one of the bleakest in the Bible: two sons so wicked that the LORD slew them, a daughter-in-law wronged, a disguise at the gate of Enaim, and Judah pronouncing a death sentence on a woman he had wronged himself. Nothing in it is presented as a model, and the root of it is in the second verse. Marriage in Scripture is a covenant made under God, not a transaction begun by sight.

The other Shuah gives the counterweight. Abraham's sons by Keturah were given gifts and sent away eastward, and one of their descendants, Bildad the Shuhite, turns up centuries later arguing theology with Job. Meanwhile the ruined chapter in Judah's life produced Pharez, and Pharez stands in the genealogy of Christ, with Tamar named in Matthew 1 among the women. God does not excuse what Judah did; he works through it and beyond it, and puts the record in the book so that no one may imagine the line to the Messiah ran through respectable people.

pos: n. (proper, a son of Abraham by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew Yoqshan, a fowler or ensnarer. He is the second of Keturah's six sons, and his line produced Sheba and Dedan — names that reappear in the prophets among the trading peoples of Arabia.
biblical_def: Genesis lists him among the sons of Abraham's later marriage: “And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah” (Genesis 25:2), and traces his line one generation further: “And Jokshan begat Sheba, and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim” (Genesis 25:3). The Chronicler repeats it, and adds the term the historian uses for Keturah's standing: “Now the sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bare Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. And the sons of Jokshan; Sheba, and Dedan” (1 Chronicles 1:32). Abraham's posterity was enormous — Ishmael's twelve princes, Keturah's six sons and their peoples, Esau's dukes — and through all of it the promise ran in one line only. Isaac was the son of the promise, and Genesis says Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a son of Abraham by Keturah, the father of Sheba and Dedan.
webster_full: POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, and so on indefinitely; the race that proceeds from a progenitor.
PROMISE, n. In theology, a declaration of God engaging to bestow a blessing, laid hold of by faith.
SEED, n. The offspring; progeny; descendants; in Scripture, especially the promised seed of Abraham.
DEDAN, n. An Arabian people and trading nation, named in Genesis and by the prophets.
SHEBA, n. A region of southern Arabia, celebrated for gold, spices and precious stones.

1 Chronicles 1:32
Now the sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bare Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. And the sons of Jokshan; Sheba, and Dedan.
Genesis 25:5
And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.
corruption_summary: Divine election is felt as arbitrary exclusion, and Genesis 25 is exactly the sort of chapter that provokes the objection: many sons, gifts to all, and the inheritance to one.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 25 states the offence plainly and does not soften it. Abraham had many sons; Keturah bore him six, of whom Jokshan is one, and they became nations. And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac. The other sons received gifts and were sent away eastward. Paul takes up this very pattern in Romans 9 — in Isaac shall thy seed be called — and anticipates the objection word for word: is there unrighteousness with God? His answer is that mercy is mercy precisely because it is not owed, and that the potter has power over the clay.

What is easily missed is how much the non-elect lines receive. Jokshan's sons became Sheba and Dedan, trading peoples with gold and spices whom the prophets name repeatedly; Ishmael got twelve princes. God is generous to those outside the line of promise, and Scripture records the generosity in detail. What Isaac had that they did not was the covenant, and the covenant was never a reward for merit. The gospel's answer to the objection is not that the promise is widened by human worth but that in Christ the blessing of Abraham comes on the Gentiles, and the line that narrowed to one opens to all nations.

pos: n. (proper, a son of Ishmael; Hebrew, a hearing or report)
etymology: Hebrew Mishma, from shama, to hear — a hearing, a report. The root is the one in Ishmael, God will hear, and in the Shema of Deuteronomy 6: Hear, O Israel.
biblical_def: He stands among the twelve princes of Ishmael: “And Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa” (Genesis 25:14), repeated in the Chronicler's roll: “Mishma, and Dumah, Massa, Hadad, and Tema” (1 Chronicles 1:30). A second Mishma belongs to Simeon's line: “Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son” (1 Chronicles 4:25) — the same names, Mibsam and Mishma, appearing in both the Ishmaelite and the Simeonite lists, which is likely a mark of intermarriage between the two peoples. The name itself is a small sermon. Hagar was told in the wilderness to call her son Ishmael, because the LORD hath heard thy affliction, and a generation later she has a grandson named a hearing. The household that God heard when it had nothing kept the memory of it in its children's names.

MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; anything that serves to keep in memory.

corruption_summary: Prayer is widely thought of as a technique for changing outcomes, and its plainest biblical ground is overlooked — that God hears, and heard a runaway bondwoman in a desert before anyone had prayed at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the root of the name. Hagar fled from Sarai into the wilderness, and the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain and said, Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the LORD hath heard thy affliction. No prayer is recorded. She was heard in her affliction before she asked, and the name she gave her son announced it for a lifetime. Two generations on, a grandson is called Mishma — a hearing — and the family memory holds.

Two things follow. The first is that God's hearing is not limited to the covenant line: Hagar was an Egyptian bondwoman with no standing, and she named God Thou God seest me. The second is that names in Scripture are theology carried in ordinary speech. A household that calls its children Ishmael and Mishma is confessing, every time it calls them in to supper, that God hears. Modern piety could stand to borrow the habit of embedding what it believes into the plainest furniture of daily life.

pos: n. (proper, a grandson of Abraham by Keturah; Hebrew, a calf)
etymology: Hebrew Epher, a young deer or calf. Two men bear it: a son of Midian in the line of Keturah, and a man in the genealogy of Judah in Chronicles.
biblical_def: The line of Keturah is traced two generations: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah” (Genesis 25:4), which the Chronicler repeats almost verbatim: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Henoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these are the sons of Keturah” (1 Chronicles 1:33). Midian is the significant name in that list. It is the people among whom Moses spent forty years, whose priest Jethro gave him a wife and, later, the best administrative counsel in the Pentateuch; and it is the people whose princes Gideon pursued and whose day of slaughter Isaiah remembers. A second Epher appears among the sons of Ezra in Judah's register (1 Chronicles 4:17). The genealogies keep both, because a register that drops the ordinary man is no register.

corruption_summary: Wisdom is expected only from inside the household of faith, and Scripture records Israel's best piece of practical governance coming from a Midianite priest who told Moses he would surely wear away.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The instructive thing about Epher's line is where it leads. The sons of Midian are Keturah's grandsons, sent east away from Isaac, and out of Midian comes Jethro, the priest who heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel, rejoiced, offered sacrifice, and then watched Moses judge the people from morning to evening and told him plainly: The thing that thou doest is not good. Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou, and this people that is with thee: for this thing is too heavy for thee. The elders, the rulers of thousands and of hundreds, the whole structure of delegated judgment, came from that conversation.

Two guardrails belong here, because Midian is also the nation whose daughters seduced Israel at Baal-peor and against whom God commanded war. Common grace is real, and the church should receive good counsel about ordering her work wherever it comes from; but doctrine and worship are not open to the same borrowing, and Midian is the standing proof that a people who gave wise counsel in one generation led Israel into whoredom in another. Take the counsel; keep the pattern of worship from God alone.

pos: n. (proper, a nephew of Abraham; also an Arabian people)
etymology: Hebrew Buwz, contempt or scorn. Abraham's brother Nahor gave the name to a son, and the people descended from him appear in Jeremiah's cup of fury among the nations in the utmost corners.
biblical_def: News came to Abraham after the binding of Isaac that his brother had a household: “Huz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of Aram” (Genesis 22:21). The list ends with Bethuel, who begat Rebekah, and it is the hinge that supplies Isaac a wife. Buz appears again as a people under judgment: “Dedan, and Tema, and Buz, and all that are in the utmost corners” (Jeremiah 25:23) — in the list of nations made to drink the cup of the LORD's fury. And a Buz stands in a Gadite pedigree: “the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz” (1 Chronicles 5:14). Elihu, the youngest of Job's counsellors and the only one God does not rebuke, is called the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram. A name meaning contempt is thus attached to a family out of which came a wife for Isaac and the man who spoke last and best before the LORD answered out of the whirlwind.

UTMOST, a. Extreme; being in the greatest or highest degree; farthest; most remote.

Job 32:2
Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God.
corruption_summary: Youth is either dismissed as having nothing to say or flattered as having everything to say; Elihu the Buzite waited because he was young, spoke last, and is the one counsellor God never rebukes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the name. The principle worth drawing out belongs to the Buzite of the book of Job. Elihu is introduced as the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram, and the narrator explains his silence: Now Elihu had waited till Job had spoken, because they were elder than he. He deferred to age, listened through thirty chapters, and then spoke — and when the LORD answered out of the whirlwind and rebuked Eliphaz and his two friends, Elihu was not named among them.

Both modern errors miss that. One tells the young that experience is everything and their judgment worthless; the other tells them that age has nothing to teach and deference is servility. Elihu did neither. He honoured the elders by waiting and then said what he believed to be true, with fear of God and without flattery of any man — let me not, I pray you, accept any man's person, neither let me give flattering titles unto man. A name meaning contempt sits over the one counsellor in the book who was neither contemptuous nor contemptible.

pos: n. (proper, a Hittite; also a son of Simeon; Hebrew, whiteness)
etymology: Hebrew Tsochar, whiteness or tawny. Two men: the father of Ephron the Hittite, from whom Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah, and a son of Simeon who went down into Egypt.
biblical_def: The first Zohar is named in the most carefully documented purchase in Genesis. Abraham, standing among the sons of Heth with Sarah unburied, asks: “If it be your mind that I should bury my dead out of my sight; hear me, and intreat for me to Ephron the son of Zohar” (Genesis 23:8). He refused to take the field as a gift and weighed out four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant, before witnesses in the gate. Years later the same field receives Abraham himself: “And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is before Mamre” (Genesis 25:9). The second Zohar is in Simeon's list: “And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar” (Genesis 46:10). One name, two men, and the first attached to the only piece of the promised land Abraham ever owned.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the father of Ephron the Hittite, and as a son of Simeon.
webster_full: MACHPELAH, n. The field and cave near Hebron which Abraham purchased of Ephron the Hittite for a burying place.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; a place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.
DEED, n. A writing containing a contract, sealed and delivered to the party; an instrument conveying real estate.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveller; particularly, one that travels to a distance from his own country.
scriptures: Genesis 23:8
And he communed with them, saying, If it be your mind that I should bury my dead out of my sight; hear me, and intreat for me to Ephron the son of Zohar,
Genesis 25:9
And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is before Mamre;
Genesis 46:10
And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman.
Genesis 23:16
And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.
corruption_summary: Faith is often set against ordinary legal care, as though a believing man should be casual about contracts; Abraham weighed the silver publicly and got a deed to a grave in a land God had already promised him.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 23 is a chapter of scrupulous commerce, and it is there on purpose. Abraham had God's promise of the whole land; he owned none of it. Ephron offered the field as a gift, in the eastern manner, and Abraham refused — he bowed, he insisted, and he weighed to Ephron the silver, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant, in the audience of the sons of Heth, at the gate. Faith did not make him careless about title; it made him careful, because he intended his children to hold that cave, and they did — Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob were all buried there.

The deeper point is the one Hebrews makes: these all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. The only soil Abraham ever owned in Canaan was a grave, bought from a Hittite at full price. A man who is sure of a country God has promised can afford to be honest and unhurried about the little he holds now — and he buries his dead in ground he has paid for, in a land he is still waiting to inherit.

pos: n. (proper, a duke of Edom; Hebrew, rest or quietness)
etymology: Hebrew Nachath, rest, quietness, a descending. A grandson of Esau by Reuel, he is one of the dukes of Edom; the name is also borne by a Kohathite and by a Levite overseer under Hezekiah.
biblical_def: Genesis 36 is the chapter of Esau's greatness, and it is meticulous: “And these are the sons of Reuel; Nahath, and Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah: these were the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife” (Genesis 36:13). The same men are then titled: “And these are the sons of Reuel Esau's son; duke Nahath, duke Zerah, duke Shammah, duke Mizzah: these are the dukes that came of Reuel in the land of Edom” (Genesis 36:17), and the Chronicler repeats the list (1 Chronicles 1:37). The chapter also observes that these kings reigned in the land of Edom before there reigned any king over the children of Israel. Esau — who sold his birthright for a mess of pottage and could find no place of repentance though he sought it carefully with tears — had dukes and kings generations before Jacob's line had one. A name meaning rest stands in the roll of a people who had earthly settlement and no covenant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a son of Reuel and a duke of Edom, and as the name of Levites in Chronicles.
webster_full: DUKE, n. In Scripture, the chief of a family or tribe, as among the Edomites; a leader or chieftain.
EDOM, n. The country and the descendants of Esau, south and east of the Dead sea.
BIRTHRIGHT, n. Any right or privilege to which a person is entitled by birth; the right of the firstborn.
REST, n. Cessation of motion or action of any kind; quiet; repose; a state free from motion or disturbance.
PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise.
scriptures: Genesis 36:13
And these are the sons of Reuel; Nahath, and Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah: these were the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife.
Genesis 36:17

And these are the sons of Reuel Esau's son; duke Nahath, duke Zerah, duke Shammah, duke Mizzah: these are the dukes that came of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife.
1 Chronicles 1:37
The sons of Reuel; Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.
Hebrews 12:16
Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
corruption_summary: Prosperity is read as evidence of God's approval, and Genesis 36 quietly refutes it: Esau's line had dukes and kings long before Israel, and Esau is the New Testament's example of a profane man.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 36 is a whole chapter of Esau's success. Dukes by name, kings in order, a settled territory, wealth enough that Esau and Jacob could not dwell together because their substance was too great. Meanwhile Jacob's family is heading toward slavery in Egypt. Anyone reading outcomes as a scoreboard would draw the obvious conclusion, and it would be exactly wrong. Hebrews warns against any profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright, and the prosperity of his descendants alters nothing about that verdict.

The name is part of the lesson. Nahath means rest, and Edom had rest of a kind — land, order, chieftains, a settled country early. The rest Scripture cares about is another thing entirely: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. Jacob's line got the covenant, the wandering, the furnace and the promise. A man may have every appearance of settlement and be profane; a man may have nothing settled and be an heir. The corrective is to stop reading circumstances as verdicts and to read the word of God instead.

pos: n. (proper, a duke of Edom; Hebrew, eloquent or a speaker)
etymology: Hebrew Owmar, from amar, to say — eloquent, a speaker. He is a son of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau, and therefore a nephew of the Eliphaz who is not to be confused with Job's Temanite friend.
biblical_def: The sons of Esau's firstborn are listed: “And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz” (Genesis 36:11), and then given their titles: “These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz” (Genesis 36:15). The Chronicler repeats the roll and adds two names: “The sons of Eliphaz; Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek” (1 Chronicles 1:36). Two of Omar's brothers matter enormously in later Scripture. Teman gives his name to the region from which Eliphaz the Temanite came to sit with Job, and Habakkuk sees God coming from Teman. Amalek, born of the concubine Timna, becomes the nation with whom the LORD swore he would have war from generation to generation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a son of Eliphaz and a duke of the sons of Esau in the land of Edom.
webster_full: ELOQUENT, a. Having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation.
DUKE, n. A chief; a leader; in Scripture, the head of a family or clan among the Edomites.
TEMAN, n. A district of Edom, proverbial for wisdom; the home of Eliphaz the Temanite.
AMALEK, n. A grandson of Esau, and the nation descended from him, the first of the nations to fight Israel.
CONCUBINE, n. A woman who cohabits with a man without being his lawful wife; a secondary wife.
scriptures: Genesis 36:11
And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz.
Genesis 36:15
These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz,
1 Chronicles 1:36
The sons of Eliphaz; Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek.
Exodus 17:16
For he said, Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
corruption_summary: Genealogies are skipped as filler, and with them the way Scripture quietly explains where later enemies came from — Amalek appears in a family list long before he appears in a battle.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What Omar's list teaches is how to read the registers. Five names in Genesis 36:11, of which Omar is one, and two more in the Chronicler's version: Timna and Amalek. Genesis explains that Timna was concubine to Eliphaz and bare him Amalek. That single clause in a skipped chapter is the origin of the nation that attacked the rear of Israel's column at Rephidim, picking off the feeble and the weary, and of whom the LORD said the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.

Teman, in the same list, runs the other way. It becomes a byword for wisdom — Jeremiah asks whether counsel is perished from Teman — and supplies Eliphaz the Temanite, the eldest of Job's comforters, and Habakkuk's vision of God coming from Teman with his glory covering the heavens. One father, one family list, and out of it comes both a proverb for wisdom and the archetype of the enemies of God's people. A reader who skips the genealogies loses the explanation of half the Old Testament's conflicts.
